cards.title: Set SMS campaign frequency to 1–2 sends per week maximum
cards.summary: SMS hits the phone's primary app with a ding, so send far less often than email—one message per week as the default, occasionally two—to protect a hard-won list from unsubscribes.
cards.use_when: Deciding your monthly SMS campaign cadence and how many messages to schedule per week for your store's list.
steps: Treat 1 SMS per week as your standing default and 2 per week as the rare exception, reserving extra sends for big events.

Recognize SMS is more intrusive than email because it triggers a notification sound and vibration in a primary app; the source says it is not comparable to sending 4–5 emails per week without backlash.
Use segmentation and selective sending so only the relevant portion of the list gets each message, reducing annoyance while keeping total weekly volume low.
Watch unsubscribe rate as your primary guardrail: the source reports unsubscribe rates on SMS run much higher than email, and that they rise the more you send.
Plan a regular monthly cadence of roughly 1–2 sends per week rather than blasting everything at a launch and going silent.
caveats: The 1–2 per week figure is the presenter's tested recommendation, not an industry standard; test against your own unsubscribe and revenue data.
Back-to-back daily sends (e.g., flash sale launch day then last-chance day) are acceptable for major events per the source.

cards.title: Keep SMS copy under 160 characters to avoid double billing
cards.summary: A single SMS segment is 160 characters; crossing that line splits the message into two and doubles your cost, and you would need roughly 2x revenue to justify it.
cards.use_when: Writing and editing SMS campaign or flow copy before sending, to control per-message cost.
steps: Count characters in the full message body, including spaces and the URL, and keep the entire send at or under 160 characters.
Understand the billing mechanic: at 161 characters the message becomes two SMS segments and you are charged for two; additional 160-character blocks keep multiplying the cost.
Judge any overage against ROI: if you send two segments you need roughly double the revenue from that message for the same return, which the source says is very rare.
Cut ruthlessly—state one simple point and a link; the source argues SMS performance comes from when and what you send, not from intricate copy.
Track which messages crossed the limit and what they earned, so you can see whether the extra segment ever paid off.
caveats: The 160-character figure is the standard SMS segment size described in the source; multi-part concatenation can change exact limits (e.g., with certain encodings), so verify with your provider.
This is the source's cost-efficiency advice, not a claim that long messages never convert.

cards.title: Limit emojis in SMS because each consumes 35–50 characters
cards.summary: An emoji can eat a third of your 160-character SMS budget, pushing you over the segment limit and into double billing, so use them sparingly or not at all.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to include emojis in SMS campaign or flow copy to add visual interest without images.
steps: Before adding an emoji, mentally subtract 35–50 characters from your 160-character budget per emoji and rewrite the rest of the message to fit.
Question the need: since MMS images are expensive, emojis are tempting as a visual substitute, but the source advises staying away from them as much as possible.
If you must use one, place it where it replaces several words rather than adding to a message already near the limit.
Audit sent messages for character-limit breaches that were caused by emoji count, and check whether the extra segments earned enough revenue to justify the cost.
caveats: The 35–50 character cost per emoji is the presenter's stated figure based on their testing; exact encoding cost can vary by emoji and platform, so verify in your SMS tool.
This is a cost-control recommendation, not a rule that emojis hurt conversion.

cards.title: Reserve MMS images for campaigns where they earn 2–3x the SMS revenue
cards.summary: MMS (image) messages cost 2–3 times more than plain SMS, so include a picture only when the message can plausibly generate two to three times the revenue of a text-only send.
cards.use_when: Choosing between a plain-text SMS and an image MMS for a product launch or campaign send.
steps: Default to plain-text SMS for your regular campaign and flow sends, since SMS itself is already far more expensive than email per message.
Before attaching an image, estimate whether the MMS send must produce 2–3x the revenue of the SMS version to break even on cost—the source says this is rarely achieved by one image.
Restrict MMS to situations where the visual is essential (e.g., a highly visual product drop) and you can defend the cost with expected revenue.
Compare MMS vs SMS versions of similar sends over time in your dashboard to see whether images genuinely lift response for your audience before scaling them up.
caveats: The 2–3x cost multiplier is the presenter's stated range; your provider's rate card may differ, so confirm actual per-message pricing.
The source's advice is to stick to SMS as much as possible, but treats MMS as a judgment call rather than a prohibition.

cards.title: Choose an SMS platform that consolidates with your existing email stack
cards.summary: Most SMS platforms do the same core things at similar prices, so pick one—ideally the same tool you already use for email—and ignore marginal AI feature comparisons.
cards.use_when: Selecting or switching an SMS provider for your store before building flows and campaigns.
steps: Check whether your current email platform also offers SMS; the source recommends Klaviyo users stay on Klaviyo to consolidate marketing in one place.
If considering alternatives, the source names Attentive and Postscript as solid options alongside Klaviyo.
Discount vendor comparisons built on novel AI features—the source argues these features are rarely used and the differences are marginal.
Note that the main platforms are similarly priced, so switching to save money is often not the deciding factor.
Expect the provider to support a dedicated phone number, data tracking, and automation setup; follow the provider's own setup guide, which the source says takes minutes.
Verify current pricing, feature sets and setup steps directly with the vendor, as these change.
caveats: The named tools reflect the source's opinion at time of recording; verify current capabilities and pricing.
There is no single 'correct' platform per the source—consolidation and simplicity are the main criteria.

cards.title: Grow the SMS list with a post-purchase opt-in checkbox
cards.summary: Add a marketing opt-in checkbox at checkout so every buyer passively contributes a phone number, giving you a growing list in the background.
cards.use_when: Setting up checkout and post-purchase list growth to continuously add SMS subscribers without extra traffic.
steps: Place a checkbox on the purchase/checkout page asking the buyer to agree to receive marketing messages.
Keep it on for all buyers so the list grows automatically with every order.
Position SMS opt-in alongside email opt-in so the same checkout flow captures both channels.
Treat this as the low-effort baseline channel; the source still calls pop-ups the most effective list-growth method, so run both.
Confirm your checkout and SMS platform support the consent capture and that opt-ins sync to the right list.
caveats: Post-purchase opt-ins yield fewer subscribers than a well-optimized pop-up per the source; they are a background contributor, not the main driver.
Consent and messaging regulations vary by region—confirm compliance for your markets.

cards.title: Delay the SMS/email pop-up trigger to 6–10 seconds after page load
cards.summary: Trigger signup pop-ups on a 6–10 second time delay—not scroll or exit intent—to maximize views without hurting site conversions.
cards.use_when: Configuring the trigger and display rules of a website pop-up form that captures email and SMS subscribers.
steps: Set the pop-up trigger to a time delay of about 6–10 seconds after the page loads, which the source says is not too soon and has been tested.
Avoid scroll-based or exit-intent triggers, which the source says can misfire; a simple time delay performs reliably.
Reject long delays: the source argues few visitors stay 30 seconds, so waiting that long means few people ever see the form.
Balance intrusiveness: the form should be seen by as many visitors as possible without harming website conversions, which is the stated fine line.
Monitor both form conversion rate and overall site conversion rate after launch to confirm the delay is not hurting purchases.
caveats: The 6–10 second window is the presenter's tested recommendation for their client set, not a universal optimum; test on your own traffic.
Pop-up timing interacts with page speed and device type—validate on mobile specifically.

cards.title: Build a two-step micro-commitment pop-up: email first, then phone
cards.summary: Ask for email in step one, then prompt for the phone number in step two with benefit-driven copy, which the source says converts roughly ten times better than asking for both at once.
cards.use_when: Designing the multi-step flow of a website signup pop-up to capture both email and SMS subscribers.
steps: Step one: state the offer plainly ('this is what you get') and ask only for the email address.
Step two: immediately prompt for the phone number with copy that ties it to completing the offer, e.g. 'finish signing up to get your discount'.
Use as few words as possible in both steps—simplicity is emphasized repeatedly.
Never ask for birthday, product preferences, or other fields in the same step; the source says extra fields kill completion.
Offer something of value—a discount, giveaway, or free guide—since the source notes people will not hand over a phone number for nothing.
Test the two-step version against a single combined field to confirm the lift in your own funnel.
caveats: The '10x better' comparison is the presenter's claim from their testing, not an independent benchmark.
Discount offers trade margin on the first purchase; the source assumes a strong email/SMS backend recovers that margin over time.

cards.title: Aim pop-up forms at 8–10% conversion vs the 2–3% baseline
cards.summary: Most audited brands convert only ~2–3% of visitors via pop-up; optimizing trigger, offer, and form simplicity can reach 8–10%, tripling list acquisition from same traffic.
cards.use_when: Benchmarking and improving the conversion rate of your site's email/SMS signup form against typical performance.
steps: Measure your current pop-up conversion rate (new subscribers divided by visitors who saw the form) to establish a baseline.
Compare against the source's observed baseline: most audited brands sit around 2–3%.
Apply the levers that drive the source's 8–10% results: a 6–10 second time delay, a strong offer, minimal copy, and the two-step email-then-phone flow.
Track the form's impact on total site conversion so you can confirm the extra visibility is not costing more sales than it creates.
Re-test offer strength separately from form design, since the source stresses you must give people a reason to sign up.
caveats: 8–10% is an outcome the presenter reports from their own optimization work, not a guaranteed result; it is a target, not a promise.
Results depend on traffic source, offer, and audience; poor-fit traffic may never reach those levels.

cards.title: Launch five core SMS automation flows before heavy campaign sending
cards.summary: Set up Welcome, Browse Abandonment, Cart Abandonment, Checkout Abandonment, and Win-back flows, keeping each short and high-ROI, since automations run in the background and earn clicks without extra effort.
cards.use_when: Building the automated SMS flow system for a store, or deciding which flows to prioritize first.
steps: Welcome flow: deliver the promised discount to new subscribers in about 2–3 SMS messages.
Browse abandonment: message users who viewed a product and left, prompting them to return and finish.
Cart abandonment and checkout abandonment: remind people who added to cart or reached checkout to complete the order with a direct link.
Win-back: re-engage customers who purchased months ago and have not returned, optionally with a discount.
Keep flow volume light—do not overload customers with messages, since flows are meant for quick, high-converting, high-ROI touches rather than retention nurturing.
Use your platform's templates and connect it to your store platform (e.g., Shopify) so triggers fire automatically; the source says setup is easy and templates exist for base flows.
caveats: The source says you 'really don't need too much' in flows—avoid adding many extra steps.
Template copy and trigger names may change in the platform interface; verify current setup steps in your tool.

cards.title: Keep SMS campaigns transactional, urgent, or announcement-based—not nurture
cards.summary: SMS campaigns should carry product drops, special offers, restocks, and announcements; pure nurture or social-proof content tends to get high unsubscribes and poor ROI on SMS.
cards.use_when: Choosing what content types belong in the SMS campaign calendar versus what should stay in email.
steps: Assign to SMS: product drops and launches, flash sales, special offers, back-in-stock/restock alerts, and important announcements.
Assign to email: nurture, educational, and social-proof content; the source says email is where you can nurture without annoying people.
Use angles that manufacture importance where relevant, e.g. a 'back in stock' message, since urgency fits the channel.
Send mostly transactional-style content on SMS and reserve the bulk of relationship-building content for email.
Cut any SMS campaign type that historically shows high unsubscribes and weak ROI in your own data, since the source found nurture/social-proof SMS underperformed.
caveats: This reflects the presenter's tested experience; your audience may tolerate more or less nurture content, so test.
Some announcement types (e.g., giveaways to grow social) are used as filler, not core revenue drivers.

cards.title: Model the SMS month around launches and flash sales, then fill the gaps
cards.summary: Anchor the SMS calendar on big events—product launches get 2–3 messages, flash sales get 2—then insert 2–3 filler campaigns (giveaway, restock) to keep a 1–2 per week cadence.
cards.use_when: Planning a store's monthly SMS campaign calendar around known launch and promotion dates.
steps: List the month's main events first; use the source's example of a brand with a Halloween product launch mid-month and a Halloween flash sale on the last two days.

For a product launch, plan about 2–3 messages: an announcement on launch day (likely the biggest sales driver), a reminder or low-stock/urgency message about a week later, and optionally a teaser 1–2 days before to build hype.
For a flash sale, send two messages: a launch message on day one and a last-chance message on the final day; the source says back-to-back daily sends are fine for big events.
Identify gaps of more than a week without an SMS and insert 2–3 filler campaigns, e.g. a social media giveaway driving to Instagram, or a 'restock' alert for a popular item.
Note the source's rationale for restock sends: an item that sold out proves popularity, and the restock itself creates urgency—you can even run one on an item that was not literally out of stock.
Count total sends against the 1–2 per week ceiling and trim if the calendar exceeds it.
caveats: The example calendar is an illustration for an eight-figure brand, not a template that fits every store size or category.
The suggested restock angle may not be appropriate if it misrepresents inventory availability.

cards.title: Test SMS send times; default to 11 a.m.–2 p.m. and 4–5 p.m.
cards.summary: There is no universal best send time, so test per audience; the source's safer windows are midday and early evening, avoiding pre-10 a.m. and post-7:30 p.m.
cards.use_when: Scheduling SMS campaigns and last-chance messages to maximize open and click response for your specific list.
steps: Run your own tests across times of day, since the source says every audience differs and there is no single right answer.
Use 11 a.m.–2 p.m. as the safest default window, when people are between morning and lunch.
Try early evening at 4–5 p.m. as a secondary window that the source says performs well.
Avoid sending before 10 a.m. (people sleep in) and after about 7:30 p.m. (people go to bed or turn off phones).
Schedule last-chance messages around 6–7 p.m. with a short deadline like '4 hours left', but not later than that window.
Track clicks and revenue by send hour over multiple sends before locking in a standard time.
caveats: These windows are the presenter's tested heuristics, not universal laws; confirm with your own A/B timing tests.
Timezone spread in your list can blur results—segment or schedule per timezone where your platform allows.

cards.title: Treat the SMS list as a channel asset for revenue you control
cards.summary: The source frames SMS as a near-guaranteed-seen channel with very high open rates and an owned list—unlike ad accounts that platforms can shut down—and reports major contribution to store revenue.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to invest budget and team time in building an SMS channel versus relying solely on paid acquisition.
steps: Evaluate SMS as an owned audience asset: contacts gave you their number, so they are not cold traffic and the list cannot be revoked by an ad platform.
Recognize the reach mechanic: the source cites an average 98% open rate because text messages are seen almost immediately by nearly everyone.
Expect automations to run continuously in the background after one-time setup, requiring only periodic checks and optimization.

Judge channel value against your store's revenue mix; the source cites an example brand generating $750k in 30 days from SMS (roughly 20% of total revenue) and $422k from automations alone in the same window.
Set expectations by tracking your own SMS-attributed revenue and automation click rates rather than adopting case-study numbers as targets.
caveats: The 98% open rate and the $750k/$422k figures are the presenter's cited examples, not benchmarks or promises; your results depend on list size, offer, and product.
Introductory framing of 'SMS is the future' is the presenter's opinion; treat it as a rationale for testing, not a guaranteed channel outcome.

Header. url: rights: public_reference why: Details a foundational guide to SMS marketing for e-commerce, focusing on list growth via pop-ups, technical constraints (character limits, MMS costs), core automated flows, and structuring a balanced SMS campaign calendar. modules: [EML] topics: [SMS marketing, list growth, campaign strategy] tier: 3 scope_hint: baseline

Topics. SMS marketing / Navigating the technical and financial constraints of SMS marketing. Managing message frequency to prevent high unsubscribe rates (recommending 1–2 sends per week), keeping copy under the strict 160-character limit to avoid double billing, minimizing emoji use (which consumes 35–50 characters), and restricting expensive MMS (image) messages only to campaigns where the ROI justifies a 2–3x cost increase. Establishing five core automated flows: Welcome (2-3 messages), Browse Abandonment, Cart Abandonment, Checkout Abandonment, and Win-back. list growth / Driving SMS list growth by optimizing website pop-up forms to capture 8–10% of visitors. Implementing a two-step micro-commitment strategy: first asking for an email, and then prompting for the phone number with clear, benefit-driven copy (e.g., "finish signing up to get your discount"). Delaying the pop-up trigger to 6–10 seconds to ensure optimal visibility without hurting website conversions. campaign strategy / Structuring an SMS campaign calendar centered around transactional, high-urgency, and important announcements rather than nurture content. Planning monthly sends around product launches (teaser, launch, reminder), flash sales (launch, last chance), and strategic filler campaigns like social media giveaways or "restock" alerts to maintain a cadence of 1–2 messages per week. Testing optimal send times, typically finding success in the 11:00 a.m. to 2:00 p.m. or 4:00 p.m. to 5:00 p.m. windows.

Look for. The primary nuances/constraints of SMS marketing compared to email: higher cost, strict 160-character limits, emoji character consumption (35–50 characters per emoji), and the 2–3x higher cost of MMS (images) versus SMS. The recommended SMS campaign sending frequency: 1 to 2 times per week. The recommended pop-up form time delay trigger: 6 to 10 seconds.

Skip. Promotional pitches to book a consulting call with the speaker or download the free SMS swipe file document in the description.

Scope mix. Almost all baseline.

Volume. 10 to 15.
